heading: ## 11 — #1 BAALBEK, LEBANON
text: Number one: Baalbek, in Lebanon's Beqaa Valley. Beneath the Roman Temple of Jupiter lies a stone platform. In one course of its wall sit three limestone blocks side by side: the Trilithon. Each is about nineteen metres long, and commonly estimated at around eight hundred tonnes. They were cut about two thousand years ago, from a limestone quarry nearby. Many researchers believe they were moved on timber tracks or rollers by enormous teams, using levers and capstans, giant winches turned by people or animals. And the strangest part is waiting in that quarry: even larger blocks, never finished. One, the Stone of the Pregnant Woman, is estimated at around a thousand tonnes. In twenty fourteen, German archaeologists exposed another, estimated at around sixteen hundred and fifty. Modern cranes can lift heavier loads. The real question is how Roman-era engineers did it with rope, timber, muscle and mechanical advantage, and why they left the biggest stones behind.
previous_text: Derinkuyu was carved out a basket at a time. Number one went the other way: single stones of almost unbelievable size.
next_text: Nine sites, thousands of years apart. No lost civilisation required.
